## Overview

Bahia bark scaling is a disease of grapefruit in north-eastern Brazil.
@Laranjeira2006 planted 240 young trees in 16 rows of 15, 2 m apart, beside
diseased adult trees, and inspected them every few months for five years and
less often for two more, noting when each tree first showed symptoms.
@Cunniffe2014 fitted a spatial epidemic model to that survey: a susceptible
tree is infected at a rate $\beta$ times the sum, over symptomatic trees, of an
exponential kernel $(2\pi\alpha^2)^{-1} e^{-d/\alpha}$; an infected tree shows
symptoms, and becomes infectious, at rate $\rho$; and nothing happens before the
young trees reach epidemiological maturity at $\delta$ months. Because a tree is
seen only at inspections, and only once it shows symptoms, the months at which
trees were infected and became symptomatic are not observed. They fitted the
model by Markov chain Monte Carlo with data augmentation, sampling those months
alongside the parameters.

This vignette fits the zoo's version of the model, `citrus_bark_scaling` (a
monthly-step adaptation of theirs), to the same survey, in two ways with
CellularAutomataInference: by data augmentation, with the exact likelihood of
the monthly path, and by approximate Bayesian computation, with summaries of
the survey.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using CellularAutomataInference
using Distributions
using Plots
using Random
using Statistics
```

## The survey

```{julia}
survey = citrus_survey()
insp = survey.inspections
println("inspections (months since planting): ", insp)
println("trees first seen with symptoms at each: ", survey.newly_symptomatic)
println("never seen with symptoms: ", count(ismissing, survey.first_symptomatic))
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-survey
#| fig-cap: "The survey. Left: the month at which each tree was first seen with symptoms (row 1 nearest the diseased adult trees; white, never). Right: the number of trees seen with symptoms by each inspection."
grid = [coalesce(survey.first_symptomatic[15(r - 1) + c], NaN) for r in 1:16, c in 1:15]
plot(heatmap(1:15, 1:16, grid; yflip=true, color=:viridis, xlabel="column", ylabel="row",
             title="month first symptomatic", aspect_ratio=1),
     scatter(insp, cumsum(survey.newly_symptomatic); xlabel="months since planting",
             ylabel="symptomatic trees", legend=false, color=:black,
             title="disease progress"); layout=(1, 2), size=(900, 400))
```

## The model at the source's estimates

The model's defaults are the source's posterior medians: $\alpha = 2.51$ m,
$\beta = 4.42$ m² per month, $\rho = 0.170$ per month and $\delta = 22.7$
months. Two hundred simulations of the grove from planting:

```{julia}
prob = problem_citrus_bark_scaling()
function progress(θ, seed)
    sol = solve(remake(prob; p=θ, seed); saveat=insp, save_start=false)
    return [citrus_symptomatic(u) for u in sol.u]
end
θsource = (α=2.51, β=4.42, ρ=0.170, δ=22.7)
runs = reduce(hcat, [progress(θsource, s) for s in 1:200])
band(runs, q) = [quantile(view(runs, k, :), q) for k in axes(runs, 1)]
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-source
#| fig-cap: "Two hundred simulations at the source's posterior medians (median and 90% band) against the survey."
function progress_plot(runs, title)
    plot(insp, band(runs, 0.5); ribbon=(band(runs, 0.5) .- band(runs, 0.05),
                                         band(runs, 0.95) .- band(runs, 0.5)),
         label="simulated", xlabel="months since planting", ylabel="symptomatic trees",
         title, legend=:topleft)
    return scatter!(insp, cumsum(survey.newly_symptomatic); color=:black, label="survey")
end
progress_plot(runs, "at the source's estimates")
```

## The exact likelihood

The rule of `citrus_bark_scaling` states its transition probabilities, so the
core's `path_logpdf` gives the exact probability of a monthly path of the grove.
Data augmentation needs it as a function of the months of infection and
symptoms; `citrus_loglik` computes the same number from those months directly,
in about the square of the number of trees operations instead of that times the
82 months:

```{julia}
fit = citrus_fit()
z = citrus_latent(fit)
println("citrus_loglik ", citrus_loglik(θsource, z, fit), "  path_logpdf ",
        path_logpdf(prob, citrus_path(z, prob)))
t1 = @elapsed for _ in 1:20
    citrus_loglik(θsource, z, fit)
end
t2 = @elapsed path_logpdf(prob, citrus_path(z, prob))
println("milliseconds: ", round(1000t1 / 20; digits=2), " against ", round(1000t2; digits=1))
```

## Data augmentation

The latent variables are each tree's months of infection and of first symptoms.
A tree seen with symptoms at an inspection became symptomatic after the
previous one; a tree never seen with them may have been infected or not.
`citrus_latent_step!` updates each tree's months in turn by Metropolis-Hastings,
and `DataAugmentation` alternates those sweeps with adaptive Metropolis moves of
the parameters. The priors are the source's: uniform on $[0, 1000]$ for $\alpha$
and $\beta$ and on $[0, 26]$ for $\delta$, exponential with mean 1/12 for
$\rho$. Four chains of 220,000 iterations, the first 20,000 discarded and every
tenth kept:

```{julia}
priors = (α=Uniform(0, 1000), β=Uniform(0, 1000), ρ=Exponential(1 / 12), δ=Uniform(0, 26))
function augmented(fit)
    return AugmentedModel((θ, z) -> citrus_loglik(θ, z, fit),
                          (rng, z, θ) -> citrus_latent_step!(rng, z, θ, fit), priors,
                          citrus_latent(fit; δ=20.0))
end
θ0 = (α=3.0, β=5.0, ρ=0.15, δ=20.0)
chains = sample(Xoshiro(1), augmented(fit), DataAugmentation(; parameter_steps=5, init_scale=0.05),
                MCMCThreads(), 20_000, 4; progress=false, initial_params=fill(θ0, 4),
                discard_initial=2_000, thinning=10)
da = posterior_summary(chains)
source = (α=(2.51, 1.96, 3.21), β=(4.42, 2.79, 7.31), ρ=(0.170, 0.135, 0.235),
          δ=(22.7, 17.9, 25.4))
r3(x) = round(x; sigdigits=3)
println("parameter  here: median [95%]          source: median [95%]     R-hat   ESS")
for k in keys(da)
    q = da[k].q
    println(rpad(k, 10), lpad("$(r3(q[2])) [$(r3(q[1])), $(r3(q[3]))]", 26),
            lpad("$(source[k][1]) [$(source[k][2]), $(source[k][3])]", 24),
            lpad(round(da[k].rhat; digits=3), 8), lpad(round(Int, da[k].ess), 7))
end
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-pairs
#| fig-cap: "The joint posterior: β against ρ and against α (every 20th draw of the four chains)."
draws = reduce(vcat, [c.values for c in chains])
d = draws[1:20:end, :]
plot(scatter(d[:, 2], d[:, 3]; xlabel="β (m² per month)", ylabel="ρ (per month)",
             markersize=1.5, alpha=0.4, legend=false),
     scatter(d[:, 2], d[:, 1]; xlabel="β (m² per month)", ylabel="α (m)", markersize=1.5,
             alpha=0.4, legend=false); layout=(1, 2), size=(800, 360))
```

The chains agree (R-hat near one). The medians lie close to the source's, the
infection rate a little higher and the dispersal scale a little longer, and
the intervals for $\beta$ and $\rho$ are wider, with a long upper tail of
$\rho$ paired with low $\beta$ (a tree infected later shows symptoms sooner),
and $\beta$ traded against $\alpha$.

## Does the fit reproduce the survey?

Simulations from 200 draws of the posterior, each with its own seed:

```{julia}
#| label: fig-predictive
#| fig-cap: "Posterior predictive check: simulations from 200 posterior draws (median and 90% band) against the survey; left, symptomatic trees over time; right, the median inspection at which each row first showed symptoms."
idx = round.(Int, range(1, size(draws, 1); length=200))
post_runs = Matrix{Int}(undef, length(insp), 200)
row_first = Matrix{Float64}(undef, 16, 200)
for (j, i) in enumerate(idx)
    θ = (α=draws[i, 1], β=draws[i, 2], ρ=draws[i, 3], δ=draws[i, 4])
    sol = solve(remake(prob; p=θ, seed=1000 + j); saveat=insp, save_start=false)
    post_runs[:, j] = [citrus_symptomatic(u) for u in sol.u]
    first = [something(findfirst(u -> u[t] == Int8(2), sol.u), length(insp) + 1)
             for t in 1:240]
    row_first[:, j] = [median(insp[min.(first[15(r - 1) .+ (1:15)], length(insp))])
                       for r in 1:16]
end
obs_row = [median(skipmissing(survey.first_symptomatic[15(r - 1) .+ (1:15)])) for r in 1:16]
plot(progress_plot(post_runs, "posterior predictive"),
     plot(1:16, band(row_first, 0.5);
          ribbon=(band(row_first, 0.5) .- band(row_first, 0.05),
                  band(row_first, 0.95) .- band(row_first, 0.5)),
          label="simulated", xlabel="row (1 nearest the source)",
          ylabel="median month first symptomatic"); layout=(1, 2), size=(900, 380))
scatter!(1:16, obs_row; color=:black, label="survey", subplot=2)
```

## Approximate Bayesian computation

ABC needs only simulations. The summaries are the share of trees symptomatic
at each inspection and each row's median inspection of first symptoms, the
spatial wave of the source's Figure 2c; the distance is the mean absolute
difference of each, added. Both are discrete, so many parameter sets share a
distance, and the inclusive kernel (`strict=false`) keeps particles tied at the
tolerance. Each simulation saves the states at the inspections only (`save_start=false`),
so the $k$-th saved state is the $k$-th inspection. The source's priors on
$[0, 1000]$ put almost no mass near the
posterior, so that particles drawn from them are wasted; here $\alpha$ and
$\beta$ are uniform on $[0, 20]$ and $[0, 50]$, far beyond the posterior found
above.

```{julia}
nins = length(insp)
first_inspection(sol) = [something(findfirst(u -> u[t] == Int8(2), sol.u), nins + 1)
                         for t in 1:240]
function summaries(first)
    counts = [count(<=(k), first) for k in 1:nins] ./ 240
    rows = [median(first[15(r - 1) .+ (1:15)]) for r in 1:16] ./ nins
    return (; counts, rows)
end
observed = summaries([ismissing(m) ? nins + 1 : findfirst(==(m), insp)
                      for m in survey.first_symptomatic])
function distance(sol, obs)
    s = summaries(first_inspection(sol))
    return mean(abs.(s.counts .- obs.counts)) + mean(abs.(s.rows .- obs.rows))
end
abc_priors = (α=Uniform(0, 20), β=Uniform(0, 50), ρ=Exponential(1 / 12), δ=Uniform(0, 26))
post = abc_smc(prob, abc_priors, distance, observed; tolerance=0.07, nparticles=300,
               rng=Xoshiro(2), solve_kwargs=(saveat=insp, save_start=false), strict=false, nsims_max=150_000)
abc = posterior_summary(post)
println(post)
for k in keys(abc)
    q = abc[k].q
    println(rpad(k, 4), "ABC ", r3(q[2]), " [", r3(q[1]), ", ", r3(q[3]), "]   data augmentation ",
            r3(da[k].q[2]), " [", r3(da[k].q[1]), ", ", r3(da[k].q[3]), "]")
end
```

Within its budget of 150,000 simulations the tolerance fell to about 0.09, not
the 0.07 asked for. ABC then places $\rho$ where the likelihood does, with a
wider interval, bounds $\delta$ only loosely, and cannot separate $\alpha$
from $\beta$: a shorter kernel with a higher rate gives much the same counts and
row medians, so the particles spread along a ridge. The exact likelihood, which
sees which trees were infected when and how far each was from the infectious
ones, pins both down.

## The source trees

The source's text says 25 diseased adult trees stood beside the grove; its
Figure 2a draws 30, which the model uses by default. Refitting with 25
(`sources=:text`), two chains:

```{julia}
fit25 = citrus_fit(; sources=:text)
chains25 = sample(Xoshiro(3), augmented(fit25),
                  DataAugmentation(; parameter_steps=5, init_scale=0.05), MCMCThreads(),
                  10_000, 2; progress=false, initial_params=fill(θ0, 2),
                  discard_initial=2_000, thinning=10)
s25 = posterior_summary(chains25)
for k in keys(s25)
    println(rpad(k, 4), "25 sources ", r3(s25[k].q[2]), " [", r3(s25[k].q[1]), ", ",
            r3(s25[k].q[3]), "]   30 sources ", r3(da[k].q[2]))
end
```

The posterior hardly moves: the number of source trees is not why the fit's
intervals differ from the source's.

## Summary

| Question | Answer here |
|:---|:---|
| Does the exact path likelihood equal the fast complete-data likelihood? | yes, to rounding |
| Does data augmentation recover the source's estimates? | the medians, closely; the intervals for β and ρ are wider |
| Does the fitted model reproduce the survey? | yes, within the 90% bands, though the survey runs a little slower than the median simulation in mid-epidemic and in the rows far from the source |
| What can ABC on summaries learn? | ρ, with a wider interval; δ loosely; not α and β separately |
| Do 25 source trees instead of 30 change the fit? | no |

With the source trees ruled out, the monthly steps of this adaptation (every
tree spends at least a month infected before showing symptoms, and a tree
changes state at most once a month) are the main remaining difference from the
source's continuous-time fit, and the likeliest reason for the wider intervals
of $\beta$ and $\rho$.
